title: Rules and learned patterns
goals: Execute a stated rule including its boundary
Select a rule by comparing errors on labelled examples
Explain why agreement with fitting examples does not establish performance on new cases

prerequisite.prompt: A warning uses temperature greater than 28 degrees C. What happens at exactly 28, and what must be checked before comparing a recorded number with 28?
prerequisite.answer: The warning stays off at exactly 28. Check that the reading is the intended quantity in degrees C and is relevant to the time and conditions.

vocabulary: A recorded property used as an input to a decision or model
A recorded category or target associated with an example
A boundary value used in a comparison
Choosing or adjusting a model using examples
The number of predictions that disagree with the comparison labels

lesson.title: The same rule can have different origins

blocks.text: A paper sorting task describes imaginary cards. Each card has a width in centimetres and a recorded label, narrow or wide. One person writes a rule from a design requirement: label a card wide when its width is at least 5 cm. Another person compares several candidate thresholds with labelled examples and chooses the one with fewest disagreements. Both may end up using the same threshold, but they selected it in different ways.

Executing a rule means applying it to an input. Fitting means using examples to select or adjust the rule or model. A fitted model can be very simple. We do not need a brain-like picture or a complicated computer to study the difference between selecting a rule and using it.

In this exercise the labels are supplied by the task designer. They are not a universal definition of wide, and a centimetre value alone would not determine every possible meaning of that word. State what the recorded labels mean in the task before counting disagreements.

blocks.title: How a threshold is selected and then applied
rows: Widths with supplied narrow or wide labels
Compare candidate rules by error count
Selected threshold and a new width
Prediction and a later comparison label
blocks.caption: The comparison label is available during fitting and later checking. A new prediction must be made before revealing that case's label.

blocks.text: For threshold t, our rule predicts wide when width is at least t and narrow otherwise. At least includes equality: with t=5, width 5 is wide. Changing at least to greater than changes the rule and may change the error count.

A fitting procedure also contains choices people made: the feature, candidate thresholds, label definition and way of counting errors. Calling a threshold learned does not remove human responsibility for those choices.

Apply threshold 3 to each width before checking the label. Only width 4 disagrees, so its error count is 1. Threshold 5 agrees on all four examples, so its error count is 0. Of these two candidates, this procedure selects 5. Zero disagreements here means it fits these four labels; it is not a guarantee about all future cards.

There can be ties. Threshold 6 also agrees on these four examples because 6 is included by at least. Thresholds 5 and 6 predict differently for width 5, which is absent from the fitting set. The available examples therefore do not uniquely determine how that width should be labelled. A procedure needs an explicit tie rule, and we should record the unresolved case.

Now use widths 1, 3, 5 and 7 with labels narrow, narrow, wide and wide. Compare candidates 3 and 5, using the same at least rule. Write all four predictions for each candidate before you count. This prevents a plausible-looking total from hiding a boundary mistake.

blocks.label: List the predictions and error count for each candidate. Select the lower-error candidate and state exactly what the result establishes

blocks.text: Keep this comparison separate from a final check on unseen cases. If we repeatedly choose a threshold after looking at the check answers, those cases have helped us fit the rule. They no longer provide an independent check of our finished choice.

lesson.title: A successful fit can still fail

blocks.text: Suppose a new card has width 5 and its supplied task label is narrow. The selected threshold 5 predicts wide, so it disagrees on this case. Do not erase the example to preserve a perfect score. Record the error and investigate whether the labels follow a different definition, whether measurement matters or whether width alone is insufficient.

For this week's paper task, a prediction is only a proposed category. It does not authorise a physical action. More consequential applications require additional checks and human decisions that a small fitting exercise cannot establish.

blocks.label: Explain the difference between choosing a threshold using examples and applying that threshold to a new card

workbook.title: Execute before fitting
workbook.prompt: Use wide when width is at least 5 cm. Predict the label for widths 4, 5 and 6. Then state what changes if the rule uses greater than 5 instead.
workbook.answer: At least 5 gives narrow, wide, wide. Greater than 5 gives narrow, narrow, wide. Only the equality case changes among these inputs.

workbook.title: Complete the supported comparison
workbook.prompt: Widths 1, 3, 5, 7 have labels narrow, narrow, wide, wide. For candidates 3 and 5, list all predictions using wide when width is at least the candidate. Count disagreements and select the lower-error candidate.
workbook.answer: Threshold 3: narrow, wide, wide, wide; one disagreement at 3. Threshold 5: narrow, narrow, wide, wide; zero disagreements. Select 5 among these candidates based on these examples only.

workbook.title: Make a tie visible
workbook.prompt: For the worked widths 2, 4, 6, 8 with labels narrow, narrow, wide, wide, compare thresholds 5 and 6. Give a width where they predict differently. Explain why the four fitting examples cannot decide that case.
workbook.answer: Both thresholds have zero disagreements. At width 5, threshold 5 predicts wide while threshold 6 predicts narrow. No fitting example is width 5 or otherwise distinguishes these thresholds; their equal fitting score does not establish a unique answer there.

workbook.title: Fit a new paper classifier
workbook.prompt: A fictional sorting task has lengths 2, 5, 7, 9 cm with labels short, short, long, long. Candidate rules predict long when length is at least 5 or at least 7. List predictions and errors for both, choose one, and predict a new length of 6 before any label is revealed. State one limit of your conclusion.
workbook.answer: Threshold 5 predicts short, long, long, long: one error at 5. Threshold 7 predicts short, short, long, long: zero errors. Choose 7 and predict short for 6. This fits these supplied labels among these two candidates; the new label, labels at other lengths and general performance are not established.

workbook.title: Keep the check honest
workbook.prompt: A learner sees that their final-check card was predicted incorrectly, changes the threshold to match it and reports the same card as an unseen test. Explain the problem and propose a valid next check.
workbook.answer: The revealed check label influenced the revised threshold, so it became part of development. Record the revision and use a different, unrevealed set after fixing the rule. Do not report the adapted-to case as an independent final test.

teacher.background: This is a genuine small fitting procedure: choose among candidate thresholds by empirical disagreement count. It is intentionally executable on paper. Do not equate all AI with machine learning or all handwritten rules with non-AI; the lesson isolates fitting versus execution. The fictional label convention avoids implying that size words have universal numerical definitions.
materials: Width and length cards with labels on a separate sheet
Two candidate-threshold cards for each exercise
A trace-table frame with input, prediction, supplied label and disagreement columns
sessions: Retrieve the equality boundary from the temperature rule. Compare greater than with at least.
Contrast a requirement-selected threshold with an example-selected threshold. Read the fitting and use diagram.
Work through all rows for candidates 3 and 5. Count errors only after writing predictions.
Pairs complete W1 and W2. Ask each learner to explain where the fitting decision occurs.
Show the tie between 5 and 6. Ask for an input that makes them disagree.
Complete W3 and discuss what the fitting data does not determine.
Collect W4 independently with comparison labels for the new case hidden.
Discuss W5 and the exit explanation. Save the selected rule and its known limitations.
teacher.guidedAnswer: For widths 1,3,5,7, threshold 3 predicts narrow,wide,wide,wide and has one error; threshold 5 predicts narrow,narrow,wide,wide and has zero. The choice establishes a lower fitting error among these candidates on these examples. The exit distinction is selecting a parameter using labelled examples versus keeping the parameter fixed while making a prediction on a new input.
misconceptions: A learned rule cannot be written simply
The selection procedure can fit a single threshold. Complexity is not the definition of fitting.
Zero fitting errors means the model is correct everywhere
Use thresholds 5 and 6, then input 5. Identical fitting scores leave different unseen predictions.
The label is available when predicting
Cover the new case's label until the prediction is recorded. Separate information available at fitting time from prediction time.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when both prediction lists and counts are correct, threshold 7 is selected, length 6 is predicted short and the learner limits the claim to available evidence. An arithmetic correction alone is insufficient if the fitting versus prediction distinction is missing. Retest with different lengths and thresholds after reteaching.
teacher.support: Use a number line with a closed dot at the threshold and arrows to the long or wide region. Permit oral explanation with a completed prediction table. Extension: ask learners to find every whole-number threshold tied for zero errors in the worked example and explain what a tie-breaking rule does.
